title: Plastic, Solid Waste and E-waste Rules and EPR

cards.b:
Waste rules change often, and UPSC tests the latest ones. Prelims asks about EPR, the 2022 single-use plastic ban and the 3R principle. Mains asks why rules fail on the ground.

Know each rule's year and its central idea.

Plastic Waste Management Rules 2016 (amended 2018, 2021, 2022) introduced Extended Producer Responsibility (EPR) for producers, importers and brand owners. They apply to the whole country, not only to cities. Local bodies manage collection and segregation.

The 2021 amendment banned identified single-use plastic items from 1 July 2022: plastic sticks for ice cream, earbuds, balloons, cutlery, plates and straws. It also raised the minimum thickness of plastic carry bags to 75 microns from 30 September 2021 and 120 microns from 31 December 2022.

EPR means producers are responsible for the waste of their product after use. They must collect or fund collection and recycling. The EPR Guidelines of February 2022 set categories of plastic packaging, targets for recycling and use of recycled content, and an online portal with certificates traded between firms.

The idea comes from the polluter pays principle. The Battery Waste Management Rules 2022 and E-Waste (Management) Rules 2022 also use EPR.

The Solid Waste Management Rules, 2016 replaced the Municipal Solid Wastes Rules of 2000. They apply beyond municipal areas and cover urban agglomerations and census towns. Waste must be segregated at source into wet, dry and domestic hazardous. They push composting, bio-methanation and waste-to-energy and ask for waste-picker integration.

The Swachh Bharat Mission (2014; Urban 2.0 in 2021) supports it. Landfill legacy sites like Ghazipur, Bhalswa and Okhla in Delhi are a burden.

India is among the largest e-waste producers. The 2022 Rules (effective 1 April 2023) cover more electronic items, set EPR targets and certificates for producers, and bring in registration of recyclers. They add a refurbisher category and make recyclers register, so that informal and unsafe recycling is pushed out.

Other waste streams: Bio-Medical Waste Rules 2016, Construction and Demolition Waste Rules 2016, and the Hazardous and Other Wastes (Management and Transboundary Movement) Rules 2016.

The hierarchy is Reduce, Reuse, Recycle, with Refuse and Recover sometimes added. Recycling is the lowest rung in preference after reduction. Circular economy ideas aim to keep materials in use. Biodegradable and compostable plastics need separate standards, and "oxo-degradable" claims are not trusted.

India generates around 3.5 million tonnes of plastic waste each year (CPCB estimates for 2019-20).

A ban on single-use items is easy to announce but hard to enforce, since substitutes may not be cheaper or better. Informal waste pickers do most recycling and need a place in the system. EPR can shift costs to consumers and is hard to audit.

A balanced view: combine bans on low-value items, EPR for the rest, better collection and consumer awareness.

Indore is the model for clean city ranking. Sikkim banned plastic bottles early, and several states had bag bans before the national rule. The National Green Tribunal has pushed states on landfills and plastic. India raised the issue at the UN Environment Assembly in 2022, where member states agreed to work towards a global plastics treaty (INC process, 2022 onward).

• PWM Rules 2016; ban on listed single-use plastic 1 July 2022.
  • SWM Rules 2016.
  • E-Waste Rules 2022, effective April 2023.
  • BWM Rules 2022 for batteries.
  • EPR: producer responsibility; online portal.

Prelims-style: "Extended Producer Responsibility is based on which principle?" (polluter pays). "Which year saw the ban on identified single-use plastics?" (2022).

Mains-style: "Is a ban on single-use plastics enough? Suggest a comprehensive approach." Structure: scale; rules; EPR; informal sector; alternatives; consumer role; global treaty.
